candidates.attacker_control: Attacker-controlled HTML string passed to the public API AntiSamy.scan(taintedHTML, policy) (AntiSamy.java line 93) or scan(taintedHTML, policy, AntiSamy.DOM) (lines 96-99). The attacker controls the <style> element's content, including the presence and boundaries of an inner <![CDATA[ ... ]]> section, and therefore whether the style element is materialized with multiple child nodes.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The SAX implementation (MagicSAXFilter.characters lines 97-115) appends every character event inside Ops.CSS to cssContent, so this is a DOM-path-only flaw rather than a universal one. The scanner does attempt error handling: on ScanException/DOMException/NumberFormatException the element is removed, and empty results become '/* */' - but these paths only apply to the scanned first child. The serializer (ASHTMLSerializer/ASXHTMLSerializer) escapes markup characters in text nodes, so the bypass produces CSS text, not raw markup; impact is therefore scoped to CSS rather than directly to HTML injection. Whether NekoHTML 1.9.22 actually splits the described input into multiple child nodes could not be executed or verified in this read-only review, which is the key residual uncertainty.
candidates.impact: Policy-enforced CSS filtering is bypassed in the DOM scan path: arbitrary unscanned CSS declarations/at-rules are emitted in the sanitized document. This weakens the sanitizer's core guarantee (every returned string is policy-validated) and enables CSS-factor attacks such as UI redressing/overlay and content-spoofing rules, external stylesheet loading via @import in custom embedStyleSheets policies, and legacy CSS script vectors (e.g. expression()/url(javascript:)) on browsers that still honor them. Direct script execution in current browsers is not demonstrated from source alone; the demonstrated defect is the CSS-validation bypass and the presence of unvalidated attacker content in the output.
candidates.prerequisites: Use of the DOM scan path (AntiSamy.DOM / AntiSamy.scan(html, policy)); a policy in which the style tag has action 'validate' (the shipped antisamy.xml has <tag name="style" action="validate">); and a NekoHTML parse of the style body that yields more than one child node (the configured cdata-sections behavior is the plausible mechanism, e.g. '<style><![CDATA[ ]]><attacker CSS></style>'). The SAX default path (AntiSamy.scan(html)) accumulates all character events and does not expose this specific flaw.
candidates.root_cause: In AntiSamyDOMScanner.actionValidate(), a <style> element with a matching policy rule is handed to processStyleTag() before any content traversal. processStyleTag() takes only ele.getFirstChild(), runs CssScanner.scanStyleSheet() on that single node and then overwrites that same node (firstChild.setNodeValue(cleanHTML) or "/* */"). It never iterates over ele.getChildNodes(), so any additional text/CDATA siblings are never CSS-scanned. Later, processChildren() -> recursiveValidateTag() only handles Element nodes (two special cases: comment and CDATA conversion) and returns early for non-element nodes ('if (!isElement) return;'), so the remaining text siblings are simply passed through to the serializer. The DOM parser is explicitly configured for CDATA sections ('http://cyberneko.org/html/features/scanner/cdata-sections' = true and 'scanner/style/strip-cdata-delims' = false), so a <style> body containing a <![CDATA[...]]> section can be represented as more than one child node, e.g. a CDATASection plus a trailing text node, and only the first one is validated.
candidates.title: DOM scanner validates only the first child of <style>, leaving sibling CSS nodes unfiltered
candidates.trace: scan(html) -> DOMFragmentParser.parse (cdata-sections=true, strip-cdata-delims=false) -> recursiveValidateTag -> tagRule action validate -> actionValidate -> (line 359) "style".equals(tagNameLowerCase) && policy.getStyleTag() != null -> processStyleTag(ele,parent): firstChild = ele.getFirstChild(); toScan = firstChild.getNodeValue(); scanStyleSheet(toScan); firstChild.setNodeValue(cleaned) -> remaining sibling node(s) untouched -> processChildren(ele) -> recursiveValidateTag(non-element text/CDATA node) returns early -> getHTMLSerializer(...).serialize(dom) writes the unscanned sibling content inside the <style> element in the returned clean HTML.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. The exact NekoHTML DOM node layout for '<style><![CDATA[ ... ]]>payload</style>' was not executed; the finding relies on the configured cdata-sections=true + strip-cdata-delims=false features and the code's single-getFirstChild handling. Impact depends on the consuming browser's CSS capabilities; no browser execution was performed.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper input validation / sanitizer filter bypass (CWE-20, sanitizer escape leading to CSS injection)

coverage_summary: Read all 48 repository files at least once: 29 Java sources (AntiSamy, CleanResults, InternalPolicy, Policy, model/*, scan/*, util/*, css/*) and 19 resources (pom.xml, README, .gitignore, 6 policy XMLs, 12 locale bundles). Traced the two public scan paths (SAX default and DOM), policy loading, tag/attribute validation, CSS validation/serialization, and the serializer escaping logic. Deepest review was on AntiSamyDOMScanner, MagicSAXFilter, CssScanner/CssValidator/CssHandler/ExternalCssScanner, URIUtils/XMLUtil/HTMLEntityEncoder, and the default antisamy.xml policy. No tests or git history are present in the snapshot, so fix/patch comparison was impossible.
limitations: No code execution, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were run; findings are source-evidence only and none are runtime-confirmed.

NekoHTML 1.9.22 and Batik CSS parser behavior (node splitting for CDATA inside <style>, entity handling, parsed LexicalUnit strings) could not be executed or inspected as binaries; the primary candidate depends on that behavior.
No git metadata/tests are present, so the snapshot could not be diffed against upstream or against a fixing commit; known-CVE mapping is therefore not asserted.

Policy XML files are large (77-82 KB each); the default antisamy.xml was reviewed in detail while antisamy-myspace/ebay/anythinggoes/slashdot/tinymce were searched and spot-checked, not fully line-read.
Locale resource bundles and the duplicated InternalPolicy constructors were reviewed only for security-relevant directives, not exhaustively verified key-by-key.
The SAX path's interaction with the JAXP transformer/serializer CDATA events was reasoned about statically only; related potential mXSS/CDATA-pass-through leads remain unverified.

rejected_leads.lead: MagicSAXFilter.startElement line 272 uses 'boolean isStyle = "style".endsWith(element.localpart);' instead of an equality/endsWith on the tag name
rejected_leads.reason: Genuine inverted-logic defect, but the CSS branch is only reached for tags present in the policy with action validate. No shipped policy (antisamy.xml, antisamy-ebay, myspace, anythinggoes, slashdot, tinymce) defines a tag whose name is a suffix of 'style' ('e', 'le', 'yle', 'tyle'), so no exploitable configuration is evidenced in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: MagicSAXFilter Ops.CSS branch re-emits the original cssAttributes unvalidated (lines 174-182): <style> attributes are never checked against the tag rule
rejected_leads.reason: Confirmed code smell (DOM scanner does validate style attributes), but the reachable attributes are inert HTML attributes on a <style> element; no concrete script-execution vector could be evidenced from source, so impact is below the submission threshold.

rejected_leads.lead: MagicSAXFilter accepts a 'style' attribute even when the tag's policy and global attributes do not define it (lines 293-304 add to validattributes without the attr != null check)
rejected_leads.reason: Value is still passed through CssScanner.scanInlineStyle, so the bypass only widens where a sanitized style attribute may appear; no XSS primitive demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: ExternalCssScanner fetches attacker-supplied @import URLs and commons-httpclient follows redirects (lines 108-171), and CssHandler.importStyle only matches offsite/onsite URL regexes (lines 214-281)
rejected_leads.reason: Real SSRF/DoS surface, but it is gated on the non-default directive embedStyleSheets=true (false in the shipped antisamy.xml) and on an explicit policy allowance for external imports; also redirect following is library behavior not visible in this source snapshot, so it is unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: Parameter masquerading in DOM scanner calls ele.setAttribute(nameValue, valueValue) with an attacker-controlled name (lines 341-350), which can raise an uncaught DOMException
rejected_leads.reason: Requires validateParamAsEmbed=true (present in antisamy.xml) and embed policy, but the outcome observable from source is at most an uncaught runtime exception/DoS, not script execution or data compromise.

rejected_leads.lead: URIUtils.resolveAsString / Policy.resolveEntity / Policy.getPolicy open URLs derived from policy files, and URIUtils falls back to file: URLs
rejected_leads.reason: Policy/include locations are trusted configuration, not attacker input in the documented usage; no path from untrusted HTML to these methods was found.

rejected_leads.lead: Constants.big5CharsToEncodeSet is defined but unused, while serializers use Constants.big5CharsToEncode.indexOf(charToPrint)
rejected_leads.reason: String.indexOf(int) returns the same membership result as the Set for all BMP chars in '<>"\'&', so the serializers still entity-encode all five characters; no security-relevant behavior difference.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtil.decode()/encode() only replace entities when the entire string matches (Pattern.matches over the whole input)
rejected_leads.reason: This affects trusted policy XML parsing fidelity, not attacker-controlled sanitizer input; no security impact path identified.

summary: Reviewed the OWASP AntiSamy 1.5.5-SNAPSHOT Java sources (48 files: DOM/SAX scanners, CSS scanner/validator/handler, policy model and parser, serializers, URI/HTML/XML utilities, and bundled policies). The strongest source-level issue is in the DOM scan path: AntiSamyDOMScanner.processStyleTag() sanitizes only the first child node of a <style> element and leaves every remaining sibling unvalidated, so on multi-child style elements (made possible by the parser's CDATA-section settings) attacker CSS is re-serialized verbatim, bypassing the CssScanner/CssValidator policy engine. Other suspicious areas (SAX style handling, external CSS fetching, reversed style-name check, unused constants) were assessed as weaker or unconfirmed and are listed as rejected leads.
